whyCorrect: Let h be the number of heather jars; then the number of blossom jars is h + 5, since blossom outsold heather by 5. Total sales give 9(h + 5) + 14h = 436, so 9h + 45 + 14h = 436 and 23h = 391, giving h = 17. Check: 17 heather at $14 is $238 and 22 blossom at $9 is $198, and 238 + 198 = 436.

whyWrong.A: 13 heather would mean 18 blossom, for 13(14) + 18(9) = $344 — $92 short of the total.
whyWrong.C: 22 is the number of blossom jars, the other unknown; the question asks for heather.
whyWrong.D: 25 heather would mean 30 blossom, for 25(14) + 30(9) = $620, well over $436.

commonMistakes: Attaching the "5 more" to the wrong variable, which makes the blossom count the answer instead of the heather count.
tips: Name the quantity the question asks for as your variable, then write the other quantity in terms of it.

whyCorrect: With d the setup charge per design and c the charge per copy, 3d + 120c = 402 and 5d + 90c = 450. From the first equation d = 134 - 40c; substituting gives 5(134 - 40c) + 90c = 450, so 670 - 110c = 450 and c = 2. Then d = 134 - 80 = 54, and both orders check: 3(54) + 120(2) = 402 and 5(54) + 90(2) = 450.

whyWrong.A: $26 forces the copy price to (402 - 78)/120 = $2.70, and the second order would then cost 5(26) + 90(2.70) = $373, not $450.
whyWrong.B: $42 forces a copy price of (402 - 126)/120 = $2.30, giving 5(42) + 90(2.30) = $417 for the second order.
whyWrong.C: $48 is just the difference between the two order totals, 450 - 402; that difference is not the setup price because the number of copies changes between the orders too.

tips: Once you solve for one variable, substitute back into both original equations — a wrong value usually fails the second one.

whyCorrect: The store drops 528 - 402 = 126 litres over 20 - 6 = 14 days, so it falls 9 litres per day. Starting from 528 litres on day 6, it must fall a further 528 - 150 = 378 litres, which takes 378/9 = 42 days. Those 42 days are counted from day 6, so the refill happens on day 6 + 42 = 48.

whyWrong.A: 36 is 42 - 6: the 6-day offset was subtracted instead of added.
whyWrong.B: 42 is the number of days of decline, not the day number — the count starts at day 6, not day 0.
whyWrong.D: 54 adds the 6-day offset a second time; at day 54 the store would be at 582 - 9(54) = 96 litres, already below the refill level.

commonMistakes: Treating the first reading as the day-0 reading, which shifts every answer by 6 days.
tips: Write the rule as a formula first — here 582 - 9d — then solve 582 - 9d = 150 and there is no offset left to forget.

whyCorrect: The money available for prints is what is left after both the licence fee and the publicity reserve: 1,250 - 290 - 110 = 850. Each print costs $84, so 84n must be at most 850, giving n at most 850/84 = 10.11. Since n counts whole prints, the greatest possible value is 10.

whyWrong.A: 9 prints cost $756 and leave $94 unspent, more than the $110 reserve requires — one more print still fits.
whyWrong.C: 11 prints cost $924, which exceeds $850 and eats into the $110 publicity reserve.
whyWrong.D: 13 comes from subtracting only the $110 reserve and forgetting the $290 licence fee: (1,250 - 110)/84 = 13.5.

tips: When the answer must be a whole number, always round the division down for a "greatest number" question, no matter what the decimal is.

whyCorrect: Going from 14 crates to 22 crates adds 8 crates and $261 - $173 = $88, so each crate costs 88/8 = $11. The delivery fee is then 173 - 14(11) = $19. For 30 crates the cost is 19 + 30(11) = $349.

whyWrong.A: $319 uses $10 per crate (19 + 300), which would make 22 crates cost 19 + 220 = $239, not $261.
whyWrong.B: $330 is 30 crates at $11 with the $19 delivery fee left off.
whyWrong.D: $360 uses $12 per crate; that would make 14 crates cost 14(12) = $168 plus a fee, already above $173 before any fee is added correctly.

commonMistakes: Scaling the total proportionally (multiplying $173 by 30/14), which wrongly charges the delivery fee more than once.

whyCorrect: Let d be the number of dodging changes; then there are 96 - d plain changes. Time gives 4(96 - d) + 7d = 507, so 384 + 3d = 507 and 3d = 123, making d = 41. Check: 41 dodging changes take 287 seconds and 55 plain changes take 220 seconds, and 287 + 220 = 507.

whyWrong.A: 33 comes from a slip in 4(96): using 408 instead of 384 leaves 3d = 99. Substituting 33 gives 231 + 252 = 483 seconds, not 507.
whyWrong.C: 55 is the number of plain changes — it is also what you get if you swap the 4-second and 7-second times.
whyWrong.D: 63 dodging changes with 33 plain would take 441 + 132 = 573 seconds.

tips: With two counts that sum to a known total, write the second as the total minus the first instead of introducing a second variable.

whyCorrect: Write the given line in slope-intercept form: \(4x-5y=20\) gives \(y=\frac{4}{5}x-4\) , so the slope is \(\frac{4}{5}\) . A parallel line has the same slope, so going from \((10,3)\) back to the y-axis moves 10 units left and therefore \(\frac{4}{5}(10)=8\) units down. The intercept is 3 - 8 = -5.

whyWrong.A: -13 drops 16 instead of 8 — at slope \(\frac{4}{5}\) , ten horizontal units are worth 8 vertical units, not 16.
whyWrong.B: -8 is the drop itself; the starting height of 3 at \(x=10\) was never added in.
whyWrong.D: 4 is the sign-flipped intercept of the original line \(4x-5y=20\) , which is -4 — and that is the wrong line anyway.

tips: Once you have the slope, use \(y=mx+b\) with the given point: 3 = \(\frac{4}{5}\)(10) + b.

whyCorrect: Factor the numerator: \(6x^{2}-19x+10=(3x-2)(2x-5)\) , since \(3x\cdot 2x=6x^{2}\) , \((-2)(-5)=10\) , and the cross terms give \(-15x-4x=-19x\) . Dividing by \(3x-2\) cancels that factor and leaves \(2x-5\) .

whyWrong.B: \(2x+5\) has the wrong sign: \((3x-2)(2x+5)=6x^{2}+11x-10\) , not the given numerator.
whyWrong.C: \(2x-10\) comes from dividing the constant 10 by 1 instead of by the -2 in the divisor; \((3x-2)(2x-10)=6x^{2}-34x+20\) .
whyWrong.D: \(3x-5\) pairs \(3x\) with \(3x\) , giving \(9x^{2}\) as the leading term instead of \(6x^{2}\) .

tips: Check any factoring instantly by multiplying the leading terms and the constants — both must match before you look at the middle term.

whyCorrect: The zeros of \(h\) are \(x=6\) and \(x=30\) , and a parabola peaks halfway between its zeros, at \(x=\frac{6+30}{2}=18\) . Substituting gives \(h(18)=-\frac{1}{4}(12)(-12)=-\frac{1}{4}(-144)=36\) . The leading coefficient is negative, so this vertex value is the maximum height.

whyWrong.A: 24 is the horizontal distance between the two zeros, 30 - 6, not a height.
whyWrong.C: 48 comes from dividing 144 by 3 instead of by 4.
whyWrong.D: 54 comes from multiplying 18 by 12 instead of 12 by 12 — both factors at \(x=18\) have size 12.

commonMistakes: Reading 6 or 30 as the maximum point; those are where the arch meets the springing line, where the height is 0.

whyCorrect: Set \(6{,}250\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{d}=10\) , so \(\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{d}=\frac{10}{6{,}250}=\frac{1}{625}\) . Since \(625=5^{4}\) , d = 4. Counting down decade by decade confirms it: 6,250, then 1,250, 250, 50, 10.

whyWrong.A: After 2 decades the amount is 250 micrograms.
whyWrong.B: After 3 decades the amount is 50 micrograms.
whyWrong.D: After 5 decades the amount is 2 micrograms — one step too far.

tips: When the base is a simple fraction, dividing repeatedly is faster and safer than taking logs.

whyCorrect: Set the two expressions equal: \(x^{2}+2x-15=x+5\) , so \(x^{2}+x-20=0\) and \((x+5)(x-4)=0\) . The x-coordinates are -5 and 4, and their product is -20. (You can also read the product straight off as the constant term over the leading coefficient, \(\frac{-20}{1}\) .)

whyWrong.B: -5 is one of the two x-coordinates, not their product.
whyWrong.C: -1 is the sum of the two x-coordinates, which is \(-\frac{b}{a}\) rather than the product.
whyWrong.D: 4 is the other x-coordinate on its own.

tips: For \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\) the roots multiply to \(\frac{c}{a}\) , so you can answer this without factoring at all.

whyCorrect: Undo the operations in reverse order. Multiplying both sides of \(J=\frac{5c-12}{3}\) by 3 gives 3J = 5c - 12; adding 12 gives 3J + 12 = 5c; dividing by 5 gives \(c=\frac{3J+12}{5}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{3J-12}{5}\) subtracts the 12 instead of adding it — the original expression already subtracted it, so undoing it means adding.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{5J+12}{3}\) multiplies by 5 and divides by 3, exactly reversing which number does which job.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{J+12}{5}\) never multiplies by 3, so the division by 3 in the original is left undone.

tips: Substitute a number to check: c = 6 gives J = 6, and only choice A sends J = 6 back to c = 6.

whyWrong.A: -119 corresponds to a = -3.5, which would make \(g(3)=-24.5\) , not -11.
whyWrong.B: -83 corresponds to a = -2.5, which would make \(g(3)=-15.5\) .
whyWrong.C: -72 is \(-2(36)\) with the constant 7 never added back.

commonMistakes: Assuming doubling the input doubles the output; the \(x^{2}\) term grows by a factor of 4, not 2.

whyCorrect: "Multiplied by the same factor every month" means the areas form a geometric sequence, so March, April and May are 12, 12r and \(12r^{2}\) . From \(12r^{2}=300\) you get \(r^{2}=25\) and r = 5, so April is 12(5) = 60. Check: 12, 60, 300 each multiply by 5.

whyWrong.B: 96 would need a factor of 8 from March to April, which gives 768 in May, not 300.
whyWrong.C: 150 splits the two-month factor of 25 in half (12.5) instead of taking its square root.
whyWrong.D: 156 is the average of 12 and 300, which is what you would use if the colony grew by a constant amount each month rather than a constant factor.

tips: Over two equal steps the overall factor is \(r^{2}\) , so take the square root, never half.

whyCorrect: Find the fuel first: 96 kilometres is 96/4 = 24 stretches of 4 kilometres, and each uses 5 litres, so the trip burns 24(5) = 120 litres. At $1.80 per litre that costs 120(1.80) = $216.

whyWrong.A: $150 corresponds to only 83.3 litres, less than the 120 litres the 5-per-4 rate requires.
whyWrong.B: $180 is 120 litres priced at $1.50 instead of $1.80.
whyWrong.C: $196 corresponds to about 108.9 litres, which no whole number of 4-kilometre stretches produces.

commonMistakes: Flipping the rate and computing 96 times \(\frac{4}{5}\) = 76.8 litres; the larger number, litres, goes on top for this trip.

whyCorrect: The five recorded wingspans total 68 + 71 + 74 + 74 + 78 = 365. For six birds to average 74, the six must total 6(74) = 444. The sixth wingspan is therefore 444 - 365 = 79.

whyWrong.A: 70 gives a six-bird total of 435 and a mean of 72.5.
whyWrong.B: 74 assumes a bird at the target mean keeps the mean there, but the first five average 73, so the mean would only rise to about 73.2.
whyWrong.C: 76 gives a total of 441 and a mean of 73.5.

tips: Turn every mean into a total before doing anything else — means cannot be added or averaged directly.

whyCorrect: Sunday's total is the Sunday column only: 39 + 63 + 48 = 150 loaves. Spelt accounts for 63 of them, and 63/150 = 0.42, so 42 percent.

whyWrong.A: 32% is 48/150, the share of barley on Sunday rather than spelt.
whyWrong.B: 38% uses Saturday's spelt count over Sunday's total, 58/150.
whyWrong.D: 45% divides Sunday's spelt by Saturday's total, 63/140.

commonMistakes: Using the whole-weekend total, 290, as the denominator; the question restricts to loaves sold on Sunday.
tips: Underline the row and the column the question restricts you to before touching the calculator.

whyCorrect: Two angles on the same side of a transversal between two parallel lines are supplementary, so \((5x+8)+(3x+12)=180\) . That gives 8x + 20 = 180, so 8x = 160 and x = 20. The angles are then 108° and 72° , which do add to 180° .

whyWrong.A: 10 gives 58° and 42° , a sum of 100° — it treats the angles as adding to something other than a straight angle.
whyWrong.C: 22 gives 118° and 78° , a sum of 196° .
whyWrong.D: 25 gives 133° and 87° , a sum of 220° .

commonMistakes: Setting the two expressions equal, which is the rule for corresponding angles (angles in matching positions), not for two angles on the same side between the lines.

whyCorrect: The rope is the hypotenuse and the flagpole is the side opposite the 60° ground angle, so \(\sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{\text{height}}{18}\) . Since \(\sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) , the height is \(18\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=9\sqrt{3}\) metres.

whyWrong.A: 9 is \(18\cos 60^{\circ}\) , the distance along the ground from the pole to the rope's anchor.
whyWrong.B: \(9\sqrt{2}\) uses \(\sin 45^{\circ}\) rather than \(\sin 60^{\circ}\) .
whyWrong.D: \(18\sqrt{3}\) is \(18\tan 60^{\circ}\) , which would be right only if 18 were the ground distance rather than the rope.

tips: Identify the hypotenuse first: it is always the side opposite the right angle, here the rope.

whyCorrect: The tank's capacity is 1.2(0.8)(0.5) = 0.48 cubic metres. Three-quarters of that is 0.48 times \(\frac{3}{4}\) = 0.36 cubic metres. Converting, 0.36(1,000) = 360 litres.
commonMistakes: Converting to litres before taking three-quarters is fine (480 litres, then 360), but converting and then forgetting the three-quarters gives 480.
tips: Multiply the three dimensions in metres so the product is already in cubic metres, then convert once at the end.

whyCorrect: The ratio 5 to 3 to 2 splits the batch into 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 equal parts, and feldspar is 3 of them. So 3 parts = 780 grams and 1 part = 260 grams. The whole batch is 10 parts, or 10(260) = 2,600 grams.
commonMistakes: Treating 780 grams as one part and multiplying by 10, which gives 7,800.
tips: Always find the value of a single part first; every other quantity in a ratio problem follows from it.

whyCorrect: For similar solids the lengths scale by \(\frac{20}{12}=\frac{5}{3}\) , but volumes scale by the cube of that factor, \(\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^{3}=\frac{125}{27}\) . So the larger vat holds \(486\cdot\frac{125}{27}=18\cdot 125=2{,}250\) millilitres.
commonMistakes: Scaling the volume by the length ratio alone, which gives 486 times \(\frac{5}{3}\) = 810.
tips: Length ratio k means area ratio \(k^{2}\) and volume ratio \(k^{3}\) — capacity is a volume.

whyCorrect: Every volume uses exactly 6 signatures and none were left over, so the number of volumes is 138 divided by 6. That is 23, since 6(23) = 138.

whyWrong.A: 18 volumes would use only 6(18) = 108 signatures.
whyWrong.B: 21 volumes would use 6(21) = 126 signatures, leaving 12 unused.
whyWrong.D: 27 volumes would need 6(27) = 162 signatures, more than the 138 available.

tips: Multiply your answer back by 6 — the product has to land exactly on 138.

whyCorrect: The $2 bag charge is not part of the rolls, so the rolls themselves cost 26 - 2 = $24. Four rolls at that price means one roll costs 24/4 = $6.

whyWrong.A: $5 would make the order 4(5) + 2 = $22, not $26.
whyWrong.C: $6.50 is 26 divided by 4 with the $2 bag charge never removed.
whyWrong.D: $7 comes from adding the $2 instead of subtracting it: (26 + 2)/4.

commonMistakes: Dividing before removing the one-off charge — the flat fee has to come off the total first.

whyCorrect: The unlocking fee is charged once and the hourly rate applies to all 5 hours, so the cost is 6 + 5(3.50). That is 6 + 17.50 = $23.50.

whyWrong.A: $17.50 is the hourly part alone, with the $6 unlocking fee left off.
whyWrong.B: $21.00 uses $3 per hour instead of $3.50.
whyWrong.D: $29.00 corresponds to $4.60 per hour, which is more than the stated rate.

tips: A one-time fee is added once, not once per hour — that is the whole difference between the wrong answers here.

whyCorrect: The $12 depends on how long the job takes, so it multiplies h; the $25 is charged once no matter what, so it is added on its own. That gives \(12h+25\) . Checking with h = 2: 12(2) + 25 = $49, which is two hours of work plus one call-out.

whyWrong.B: \(12h-25\) subtracts the call-out fee; the tuner charges it, so it is added.
whyWrong.C: \(25h+12\) swaps the roles, charging the call-out fee every hour and the hourly rate only once.
whyWrong.D: \(37h\) adds 25 and 12 first, which charges a fresh call-out fee for every hour worked.

tips: Ask which number changes when the job runs longer — that number is the one attached to h.

whyCorrect: After h hours the temperature is 17 + 2h, and it must stay below 24, so 17 + 2h < 24 and 2h < 7, giving h < 3.5. The greatest whole number below 3.5 is 3, and after 3 hours the room is at 23°C, still under the limit.

whyWrong.B: 4 hours puts the room at 17 + 8 = 25°C, which is above the limit — 3.5 was rounded up rather than down.
whyWrong.C: 7 is the size of the temperature gap, 24 - 17, not a number of hours.
whyWrong.D: 12 is 24 divided by 2, which ignores that the room already starts at 17°C.

tips: Test your whole-number answer in the inequality; "greatest whole number" answers always round down.

whyCorrect: Three adult tickets cost 3(9) = $27 and five child tickets cost 5(4) = $20. Together that is 27 + 20 = $47.

whyWrong.A: $39 uses 3 child tickets instead of 5: 27 + 12.
whyWrong.B: $45 is five tickets all priced as adult tickets, 5(9).
whyWrong.D: $52 prices 4 adults and 4 children, 4(9) + 4(4).

tips: Write the two products separately before adding, so neither count gets attached to the wrong price.

whyCorrect: For a cube with edge s the volume is \(s^{3}\) , so \(s^{3}=512\) and s is the cube root of 512. Since \(8^{3}=512\) , each edge is 8 feet.
commonMistakes: Taking a square root instead of a cube root, which gives about 22.6.
tips: Memorise the small cubes — 125, 216, 343, 512, 729 — and these questions become instant.

whyCorrect: Multiplying powers with the same base adds the exponents: \(t^{6}\cdot t^{3}=t^{6+3}=t^{9}\) . Writing it out shows why — six factors of t times three more factors of t is nine factors of t.

whyWrong.A: \(t^{2}\) divides the exponents, which is not a rule for any operation here.
whyWrong.C: \(t^{18}\) multiplies the exponents; that is the rule for a power of a power, \((t^{6})^{3}\) .
whyWrong.D: \(t^{63}\) simply writes the two exponents side by side.

tips: Multiply bases means add exponents; raise a power to a power means multiply them.

whyCorrect: Substitute k = 6 into \(k^{2}+3\) . That gives \(6^{2}+3=36+3=39\) tiles.

whyWrong.A: 15 comes from 2(6) + 3, treating \(k^{2}\) as 2k.
whyWrong.B: 21 comes from 3(6) + 3, multiplying by 3 instead of squaring.
whyWrong.C: 33 subtracts the 3 instead of adding it: 36 - 3.

tips: \(k^{2}\) means k times k, never k times 2.

whyCorrect: Set \(3t^{2}=108\) , so \(t^{2}=36\) and t = 6 (time cannot be negative). Check: \(3(6)^{2}=3(36)=108\) centimetres.

whyWrong.B: 12 comes from treating the expression as 3t, solving 3t = 36.
whyWrong.C: 18 halves 36 instead of taking its square root.
whyWrong.D: 36 is the value of \(t^{2}\) , stopping one step before the square root.

commonMistakes: Dividing by 3 and then forgetting that the result is \(t^{2}\) , not t.

whyCorrect: Substitute d = 8 into \(M(d)=\frac{72}{d}-1\) : \(\frac{72}{8}=9\) , and then 9 - 1 = 8.

whyWrong.B: 9 is \(\frac{72}{8}\) with the -1 never applied.
whyWrong.C: 71 subtracts 1 from 72 and never divides by 8.
whyWrong.D: 72 is the numerator, which is the value before either operation.

tips: Division comes before subtraction in the order of operations, so divide first, then take off the 1.

whyCorrect: Substitute h = 3 into \(B(h)=3\cdot 4^{h}\) . The exponent applies only to the 4, so \(4^{3}=64\) and then 3(64) = 192.

whyWrong.A: 36 comes from 3(4)(3), multiplying by 3 rather than raising 4 to the third power.
whyWrong.B: 48 is \(3\cdot 4^{2}\) , the count after 2 hours.
whyWrong.C: 144 uses \(4^{3}=48\) instead of 64.

commonMistakes: Multiplying 3 by 4 first and then raising to the power — the coefficient is not inside the exponent.

whyCorrect: Pigment is 3 parts and 45 grams, so one part is 45/3 = 15 grams. Base is 5 parts, or 5(15) = 75 grams.

whyWrong.A: 27 flips the ratio, computing 45 times \(\frac{3}{5}\) instead of \(\frac{5}{3}\) .
whyWrong.B: 60 adds a single 15-gram part to the pigment instead of taking five parts.
whyWrong.D: 120 is the total mass of the batch, pigment plus base.

tips: Find one part first; every quantity in the ratio is then a whole number of parts.

whyCorrect: Percent change compares the drop with the original price. The drop is 250 - 210 = 40, so the percent fall is 40/250 = 0.16, or 16 percent.

whyWrong.A: 14% corresponds to a drop of $35, not $40.
whyWrong.C: 19% divides by the new price, 40/210, instead of the original.
whyWrong.D: 40% mistakes the size of the drop in dollars for a percent.

commonMistakes: Using the new value as the base — for a fall, the base is always the price you started from.

whyCorrect: Read the two rows the question names: Ings is 31 and Kettle is 19. "How many more" means subtract: 31 - 19 = 12.

whyWrong.A: 7 is 31 - 24, using Hollin's count instead of Kettle's.
whyWrong.C: 19 is Kettle's own count, not the difference.
whyWrong.D: 50 adds the two counts instead of subtracting.

tips: "How many more" is always a subtraction; find both rows before you compute anything.

whyCorrect: The seven counts are already in order: 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, 6, 11. With 7 values the median is the 4th one, which has three values below it and three above. That value is 4.

whyWrong.A: 3 is the most common value, the mode.
whyWrong.C: 5 is the mean: the counts total 35, and 35/7 = 5.
whyWrong.D: 6 is the 5th value, one position past the middle.

tips: For n values in order, the median sits at position \(\frac{n+1}{2}\) — here position 4.

whyCorrect: In a parallelogram, two angles next to each other lie between a pair of parallel sides, so they are supplementary and add to 180° . The adjacent angle is therefore 180 - 62 = 118 degrees.

whyWrong.A: 28 treats the two angles as complementary, adding to 90° .
whyWrong.B: 62 is the measure of the opposite angle, which is equal, not the adjacent one.
whyWrong.D: 128 comes from subtracting 62 from 190 instead of 180.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the two parallelogram rules: opposite angles are equal, adjacent angles are supplementary.

whyCorrect: The area of a rectangle is length times width, so the allotment covers 24(15) = 360 square metres.
commonMistakes: Computing the perimeter, 2(24) + 2(15) = 78, which is a distance rather than an area.

whyCorrect: The mast, the ground and the wire form a right triangle with legs 12 and 9, and the wire is the hypotenuse. So \(12^{2}+9^{2}=144+81=225\) , and the wire is \(\sqrt{225}=15\) metres.
commonMistakes: Adding the two lengths to get 21, or subtracting to get 3; the hypotenuse comes from squares, not from the sides directly.
tips: Recognise the 3-4-5 family: 9, 12, 15 is that triple scaled by 3.

whyCorrect: In \(H(t)=1{,}200-40t\) the number 40 is multiplied by t, the number of minutes, so it is a rate: each extra minute subtracts 40 metres from the height. Since the height is falling, 40 is how many metres the balloon descends per minute.

whyWrong.B: The starting height is 1,200, the value of H when t = 0.
whyWrong.C: The time to reach the ground is 1,200/40 = 30 minutes, not 40.
whyWrong.D: 1,200 is a height, not a time you can substitute for t; at t = 1,200 the model would give a height far below the ground.

tips: In \(y=mx+b\) the coefficient of the variable is always a rate per unit of that variable.

whyCorrect: Add the two expressions, combining like terms only with like terms: \((3n+5)+(2n-8)\) gives 3n + 2n = 5n and 5 + (-8) = -3, so the total is \(5n-3\) .

whyWrong.B: \(5n+13\) subtracts the -8 instead of adding it; striking contributes -8, so the constants give 5 - 8.
whyWrong.C: \(6n-3\) multiplies the n terms instead of adding them.
whyWrong.D: \(6n-40\) multiplies both pairs of terms, which is what you would get if the two times were multiplied rather than added.

tips: Only n terms combine with n terms; constants combine with constants.

whyCorrect: Distributing means the 3 multiplies both terms inside the parentheses: 3(2m) = 6m and 3(-7) = -21, so \(3(2m-7)=6m-21\) . Checking with m = 5: 3(10 - 7) = 9, and 6(5) - 21 = 9.

whyWrong.A: \(2m-21\) multiplies only the constant, leaving 2m untouched.
whyWrong.B: \(5m-7\) adds 3 and 2 instead of multiplying them, and never touches the 7.
whyWrong.C: \(6m-7\) multiplies only the first term and leaves the 7 undistributed.

commonMistakes: Distributing to the first term and stopping — every term inside the parentheses gets multiplied.

whyCorrect: A system has infinitely many solutions only when one equation is a multiple of the other. Comparing the x-terms, 9 is \(\frac{3}{2}\) times 6, and the constants agree with that: 15 is \(\frac{3}{2}\) times 10. So the y-term must scale the same way: \(c=\frac{3}{2}(-4)=-6\) .

whyWrong.B: -4 just copies the first equation's y-coefficient, which would only work if the two equations were identical.
whyWrong.C: 4 has the wrong sign; multiplying -4 by a positive \(\frac{3}{2}\) keeps it negative.
whyWrong.D: 6 scales the coefficient correctly in size but drops the negative sign, which would make the lines intersect at a single point instead.

tips: Check the constant terms too — if they do not scale by the same factor, the system has no solution rather than infinitely many.

whyCorrect: For a linear function, a rise of 12 over a run of 3 means the slope is 12/3 = 4. Going from x = 2 to x = 11 is a run of 9, so the output rises by 4(9) = 36. Therefore \(f(11)=5+36=41\) .

whyWrong.A: 29 adds only 24, which covers two steps of 3 instead of the three steps from 2 to 11.
whyWrong.B: 36 is the increase alone, with the starting value \(f(2)=5\) never added.
whyWrong.D: 53 adds 12 four times; the gap from 2 to 11 is 9, which is three steps of 3, not four.

tips: Turn \(f(x+3)=f(x)+12\) straight into a slope before doing anything else.

whyCorrect: Making b barrels forces at least 3b firkins, and firkins are what eat the remaining time, so use the smallest allowed number of them. Staving time is then 3b + 2(3b) = 9b hours, which must be at most 96, giving b at most 96/9 = 10.67. So the cooper can make 10 barrels: 10 barrels and 30 firkins take 30 + 60 = 90 hours.

whyWrong.B: 12 barrels force at least 36 firkins, taking 36 + 72 = 108 hours — more than the 96 available.
whyWrong.C: 16 comes from charging only 3 extra hours per barrel for its firkins, but 3 firkins take 3(2) = 6 hours, not 3.
whyWrong.D: 32 is 96/3, which counts barrel time only and ignores the firkins the cooper is required to make.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that the firkin requirement is per barrel, so every barrel really costs 9 hours of staving.

whyCorrect: The margin removes w from each of the two opposite edges, so the written area is \((30-2w)(20-2w)=264\) . Expanding gives \(4w^{2}-100w+600=264\) , so \(w^{2}-25w+84=0\) and \((w-4)(w-21)=0\) . Only w = 4 fits the sheet, and it checks: 22 by 12 is 264.

whyWrong.A: 3 gives a written area of 24 by 14 = 336 square centimetres.
whyWrong.C: 5 gives 20 by 10 = 200 square centimetres.
whyWrong.D: 6 gives 18 by 8 = 144 square centimetres.

commonMistakes: Subtracting w rather than 2w from each dimension — the margin appears on both sides of the sheet.
tips: The quadratic's other root, 21, is larger than half the short side, so it is discarded.

whyCorrect: Replacing x by x - 3 shifts the graph 3 units to the right (the input must be 3 larger to produce the same output), and adding 4 shifts it 4 units up. The vertex \((2,5)\) therefore moves to \((2+3,;5+4)=(5,9)\) .

whyWrong.A: \((-1,1)\) shifts left 3 and down 4, reversing both directions.
whyWrong.B: \((-1,9)\) gets the vertical shift right but moves left instead of right.
whyWrong.C: \((5,1)\) moves right correctly but subtracts 4 instead of adding it.

commonMistakes: Reading the minus sign in x - 3 as a leftward shift; inside the function, the sign is inverted, but the +4 outside is not.

whyCorrect: Complete the square: \(3x^{2}+18x+5=3(x^{2}+6x)+5=3(x+3)^{2}-27+5=3(x+3)^{2}-22\) . Since \(3(x+3)^{2}\) is never negative, the smallest value of h is -22, reached at x = -3, and that minimum sits in the expression as the constant.

whyWrong.B: \(3(x+3)^{2}+5\) is not equivalent — factoring 3 out of \(6x\) creates a \(3(3)^{2}=27\) that must be subtracted back.
whyWrong.C: \(3(x+6)^{2}-22\) halves nothing: the number inside must be half of 6, which is 3.
whyWrong.D: \((3x+9)^{2}-22\) squares the 3 as well, giving a \(9x^{2}\) term instead of \(3x^{2}\) .

tips: Expand your completed square mentally to confirm it returns the original — that catches every one of these.

whyCorrect: Upstream the launch makes v - 2 and downstream v + 2 kilometres per hour, so the total time is \(\frac{24}{v-2}+\frac{24}{v+2}=5\) . Clearing the denominators gives \(24(v+2)+24(v-2)=5(v^{2}-4)\) , so \(48v=5v^{2}-20\) and \(5v^{2}-48v-20=0\) , which factors to give v = 10 (the negative root is discarded). Check: 24/8 = 3 hours up and 24/12 = 2 hours back.

whyWrong.C: 12 gives 24/10 + 24/14 = about 4.1 hours, too fast.
whyWrong.D: 14 gives 2 + 1.5 = 3.5 hours.

commonMistakes: Averaging the two speeds, or using 48/5 = 9.6 as the still-water speed; unequal times mean the average speed is not the still-water speed.

whyCorrect: The common denominator is \((x-3)(x+1)=x^{2}-2x-3\) . Rewriting, \(\frac{1}{x-3}-\frac{2}{x+1}=\frac{(x+1)-2(x-3)}{x^{2}-2x-3}\) . The numerator is \(x+1-2x+6=7-x\) , giving \(\frac{7-x}{x^{2}-2x-3}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{-1}{x^{2}-2x-3}\) subtracts the numerators 1 and 2 directly, without multiplying each by the other fraction's denominator.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{x+7}{x^{2}-2x-3}\) drops the -2x when distributing -2 across \(x-3\) .
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{7-x}{x^{2}-3}\) has the right numerator but multiplies the denominators as if \((x-3)(x+1)=x^{2}-3\) .

tips: Distribute the minus sign over the whole second numerator, including its x-term.

whyCorrect: Substituting the known ground point \((0,0)\) gives \(-\frac{1}{50}h^{2}+18=0\) , so \(h^{2}=900\) and h = 30. The parabola is symmetric about its vertex at x = 30, so the second ground point is as far to the right of 30 as 0 is to the left: x = 60. The two points are 60 metres apart.

whyWrong.A: 30 is the vertex's x-coordinate, which is half the span between the ground points.
whyWrong.B: 45 would put the vertex at x = 22.5, and then the peak height would be \(\frac{22.5^{2}}{50}\) , about 10.1 metres, not 18.
whyWrong.D: 75 would put the vertex at x = 37.5 and a peak height of about 28.1 metres.

tips: A parabola's two x-intercepts are always mirror images about the vertex line, so the span is twice the distance from either intercept to the vertex.

whyCorrect: Cross-multiplying gives \(x(2x-1)=3(x+4)\) , so \(2x^{2}-x=3x+12\) and \(2x^{2}-4x-12=0\) , or \(x^{2}-2x-6=0\) after dividing by 2. The sum of the roots is \(-\frac{b}{a}=\frac{2}{1}=2\) . (The roots are \(1\pm\sqrt{7}\) , neither of which is excluded.)

whyWrong.A: -6 is the product of the roots, the constant term of \(x^{2}-2x-6\) .
whyWrong.B: -2 takes the coefficient of x as the sum without changing its sign; the sum is \(-\frac{b}{a}\) .
whyWrong.D: 4 uses \(2x^{2}-4x-12\) but forgets to divide by the leading coefficient 2.

tips: Reducing the quadratic to leading coefficient 1 first makes the sum and product readable straight off.

whyCorrect: Let x be the kilograms of the 30% alloy; the rest, 44 - x, is the 8% alloy. Tin balances: 0.30x + 0.08(44 - x) = 0.15(44) = 6.6. That gives 0.22x + 3.52 = 6.6, so 0.22x = 3.08 and x = 14.

whyWrong.A: 12 kilograms of the 30% alloy with 32 of the 8% gives 3.6 + 2.56 = 6.16 kg of tin, a mixture of only 14%.
whyWrong.C: 18 kilograms gives 5.4 + 2.08 = 7.48 kg of tin, about 17%.
whyWrong.D: 30 is the percent from the problem, not a mass; 30 kilograms would push the mixture to about 23% tin.

tips: Track the tin, not the alloy — write the mass of tin contributed by each piece and set the total equal to 15% of 44.

whyCorrect: Seedlings were randomly assigned to the two mulches, which makes the two groups alike in every other respect on average, so a significant difference in growth can be attributed to the mulch. But the seedlings were all one variety in one study, so the conclusion holds only for seedlings like those studied.

whyWrong.B: "Any plant" goes far beyond the single variety that was tested; the study says nothing about other species.
whyWrong.C: Random assignment is exactly what makes a causal explanation legitimate, so ruling causation out is backwards.
whyWrong.D: The result is about averages; individual seedlings vary, and the study cannot support a claim about every one of them.

tips: Random assignment licenses cause; random selection licenses generalising to a population. Here only assignment was random.

whyCorrect: Turn the mean into a total: 12 samples averaging 47 grams weigh 12(47) = 564 grams. Removing 35 and 34 grams leaves 564 - 69 = 495 grams spread over 10 samples, so the new mean is 495/10 = 49.5 grams.

whyWrong.A: 47 assumes removing samples cannot change the mean, but both removed samples were below average, so the mean rises.
whyWrong.B: 48.5 corresponds to removing 79 grams instead of 69.
whyWrong.C: 49 corresponds to removing 74 grams, or to rounding 49.5 down.

tips: Removing below-average values always pulls the mean up — use that as a sanity check on the direction.

whyCorrect: One "unit" of mixture is 5 litres of ink plus 2 of extender, 7 litres in all. The ink allows 80/5 = 16 units and the extender allows 40/2 = 20 units, so ink is the binding limit at 16 units. That makes 16(7) = 112 litres, using all 80 litres of ink and 32 litres of extender.

whyWrong.B: 120 is simply all the ink plus all the extender, which would be a 2-to-1 mixture, not 5 to 2.
whyWrong.C: 140 uses the extender's 20 units, but that would need 100 litres of ink and only 80 are available.
whyWrong.D: 168 divides the combined 120 litres as if it were all ink, giving 24 units.

tips: With two ingredients capped, compute how many whole recipe units each one allows and take the smaller.

whyCorrect: Alder fires 14(60) = 840 pieces and loses 5%, so 0.95(840) = 798 survive. Birch fires 9(80) = 720 pieces and loses 10%, so 0.90(720) = 648 survive. The difference is 798 - 648 = 150.

whyWrong.A: 108 is 150 with Alder's 42 cracked pieces taken off a second time.
whyWrong.B: 120 is the difference in pieces loaded, 840 - 720, with neither loss rate applied.
whyWrong.D: 192 subtracts Birch's survivors from Alder's loaded total, 840 - 648, forgetting Alder's 5% loss.

tips: Multiply firings by pieces per firing first, then apply the survival percent — the percent columns cannot be compared on their own.

whyCorrect: The altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two segments it creates: \(12^{2}=9q\) , where q is the other segment. So 144 = 9q and q = 16, making the hypotenuse 9 + 16 = 25.

whyWrong.A: 16 is the longer segment of the hypotenuse, not the whole hypotenuse.
whyWrong.B: 20 is the longer leg of the triangle, \(\sqrt{12^{2}+16^{2}}\) , not the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.C: 21 adds the altitude to the short segment, 9 + 12, but the altitude is not part of the hypotenuse.

tips: Remember the relation altitude squared equals the product of the two hypotenuse pieces; it turns this into one division.

whyCorrect: If the sphere has radius r, the tin has the same radius and its height equals the sphere's diameter, 2r. So the sphere is \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\) and the tin is \(\pi r^{2}(2r)=2\pi r^{3}\) . The ratio is \(\frac{4/3}{2}=\frac{2}{3}\) , whatever r is.

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{1}{2}\) is an eyeball guess; with r = 3 the sphere is \(36\pi\) and the tin \(54\pi\) , and 36 is more than half of 54.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{3}{5}\) would need the tin to be \(60\pi\) when the sphere is \(36\pi\) , a height greater than the sphere's diameter.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{3}{4}\) inverts \(\frac{4}{3}\) and never divides by the tin's factor of 2.

tips: Set r = 1 and compute both volumes numerically if the algebra feels slippery — the ratio never depends on r.

whyCorrect: With the right angle at L, \(\cos J=\frac{7}{25}\) means the leg adjacent to J is 7 and the hypotenuse is 25. The third side is \(\sqrt{25^{2}-7^{2}}=\sqrt{625-49}=24\) , the leg opposite J. So \(\tan J=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{24}{7}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{7}{24}\) is the reciprocal, adjacent over opposite.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{24}{25}\) is \(\sin J\) — opposite over hypotenuse, not over the adjacent leg.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{25}{7}\) is hypotenuse over adjacent, the reciprocal of the cosine.

tips: Draw the 7-24-25 triangle and label the sides relative to J before choosing a ratio.

whyCorrect: Light parcels are required, so carry as few as allowed: 20 of them, weighing 20(15) = 300 kilograms. That leaves 1,400 - 300 = 1,100 kilograms for heavy parcels, and 1,100/40 = 27.5, so at most 27 heavy parcels. The parcel count is fine too: 27 + 20 = 47, under the 60-parcel limit.

whyWrong.A: 25 heavy parcels weigh only 1,000 kilograms and leave 100 kilograms of the limit unused — two more heavy parcels still fit.
whyWrong.C: 29 heavy parcels weigh 1,160 kilograms, which with the required 20 light parcels totals 1,460 kilograms, over the 1,400 limit.
whyWrong.D: 35 is 1,400/40, which uses the whole mass allowance on heavy parcels and ignores the 20 required light ones.

tips: When a minimum is forced on one item, take exactly that minimum — anything more only eats the budget for the item you are maximising.

whyCorrect: From 4 kg to 10 kg the load rises 6 and the stretch rises 21 - 9 = 12, so the spring stretches 2 centimetres per kilogram. The rule is stretch = 2L + 1, since 2(4) + 1 = 9. Setting 2L + 1 = 33 gives L = 16.
commonMistakes: Treating the relationship as directly proportional (stretch = 2.25L from the first pair) — the line does not pass through the origin here.
tips: Find the rate from the two given points first, then use one point to pin down the constant.

whyCorrect: Let d be the one-way distance. The outward ride takes \(\frac{d}{24}\) hours and the return \(\frac{d}{16}\) hours, and these total 5. Since \(\frac{d}{24}+\frac{d}{16}=\frac{2d}{48}+\frac{3d}{48}=\frac{5d}{48}\) , we need \(\frac{5d}{48}=5\) , so d = 48. Check: 2 hours out and 3 hours back.
commonMistakes: Averaging 24 and 16 to 20 km/h and computing 100 km for the round trip; the slower leg takes more time, so the average speed is below 20.

whyCorrect: The base is a square of side s, so the volume is \(9s^{2}=576\) , giving \(s^{2}=64\) and s = 8. The two square faces contribute 2(64) = 128 square centimetres and the four side faces contribute 4(8)(9) = 288, for a total of 128 + 288 = 416.
commonMistakes: Using six identical faces as if the case were a cube, which gives 6(64) = 384.
tips: Count the faces by type: two squares of side s and four rectangles s by the height.

whyCorrect: Write the two orders as 5r + 2b = 76 and 3r + 4b = 68, with r and b the milling prices per sack. Doubling the first gives 10r + 4b = 152, and subtracting the second leaves 7r = 84, so r = 12. Then 2b = 76 - 5(12) = 16, so barley costs $8 a sack.

whyWrong.B: $10 for barley forces rye to (76 - 20)/5 = $11.20, and the second order would cost 3(11.20) + 40 = $73.60, not $68.
whyWrong.C: $12 is the rye price, the other unknown in the system.
whyWrong.D: $14 forces rye to $9.60, making the second order 3(9.60) + 56 = $84.80.

tips: Scale one equation so a variable's coefficients match, then subtract — that eliminates it in one step.

whyCorrect: The stalagmite gains 445 - 412 = 33 millimetres in 2015 - 1985 = 30 years, so it grows 1.1 millimetres per year. From 445 millimetres it needs another 55 millimetres, and 55/1.1 = 50 years. That puts it at 500 millimetres in 2015 + 50 = 2065.

whyWrong.A: 2045 is only 30 years past 2015, which adds another 33 millimetres and reaches just 478.
whyWrong.C: 2075 gives 60 more years of growth, 66 millimetres, for a height of 511.
whyWrong.D: 2095 adds the correct 80-year span to 2015 instead of to 1985.

tips: Decide which reading you are measuring from before adding years — the 80-year span belongs to 1985, the 50-year span to 2015.

whyCorrect: After the licensing fee the society has 1,150 - 265 = $885 for rentals. Since 885/74 = 11.96, it can afford 11 films: 11(74) = $814, leaving $71 — not enough for a twelfth.

whyWrong.A: 9 films cost $666 and leave $219 unspent, enough for two more.
whyWrong.B: 10 films cost $740 and leave $145, still enough for one more.
whyWrong.D: 12 films cost $888, which is $3 more than the $885 available.

tips: Always multiply the rounded-down count back out and check the remainder is less than one more rental.

whyCorrect: Let b be the number of bicycles; then the foot passengers number 2b + 3. Since the two counts total 78, b + (2b + 3) = 78, so 3b = 75 and b = 25. The question asks for foot passengers: 2(25) + 3 = 53.

whyWrong.A: 25 is the number of bicycles, the variable you solved for first.
whyWrong.B: 26 is 78 divided by 3, which would be right only if the two counts were equal thirds.
whyWrong.C: 39 splits the 78 evenly, ignoring "3 more than twice".

commonMistakes: Stopping at the variable you solved for instead of the quantity the question names.

whyCorrect: The extra 5 months between the two customers cost 532 - 332 = $200, so the monthly fee is 200/5 = $40. The setup fee is what is left of the first bill after 7 months of service: 332 - 7(40) = 332 - 280 = $52. Check the second bill: 52 + 12(40) = $532.

whyWrong.A: $40 is the monthly fee, not the one-time setup fee.
whyWrong.B: $47 would make the monthly fee (332 - 47)/7 = $40.71, and 12 months would then come to about $536.
whyWrong.D: $60 would make the monthly fee about $38.86, giving about $526 for 12 months.

tips: The difference between two totals removes the one-time fee, which is why it isolates the monthly rate.

whyCorrect: Working towards each other, the crews close the gap at the combined rate 38 + 46 = 84 metres a day. They meet when the cleared lengths total 1,764 metres, so the time is 1,764/84 = 21 days.

whyWrong.A: 14 days clears only 84(14) = 1,176 metres, leaving 588 metres of path.
whyWrong.C: 24 days would clear 2,016 metres — they would already have met three days earlier.
whyWrong.D: 42 comes from using the average rate 42 metres a day instead of the combined rate 84.

commonMistakes: Averaging the two rates instead of adding them; both crews work at the same time, so the rates add.

whyCorrect: From 45 cm to 70 cm the width rises 25 cm and the thread count rises 1,740 - 1,140 = 600, so the loom uses 600/25 = 24 threads per centimetre. From 70 cm to 100 cm is 30 more centimetres, adding 30(24) = 720 threads: 1,740 + 720 = 2,460.

whyWrong.A: 2,340 adds another 600 to 1,740, treating 70 to 100 as a 25-centimetre step instead of 30.
whyWrong.B: 2,400 is 100(24), which ignores the fixed part of the rule — at 45 cm the count is 1,140, which is 60 more than 45(24).
whyWrong.D: 2,520 adds the fixed 60 threads a second time on top of 2,460.

tips: Check your linear rule against both given points before extending it.

whyCorrect: Factor the numerator: \(6x^{2}-7x-20=(3x+4)(2x-5)\) , since \(3x\cdot 2x=6x^{2}\) , \(4(-5)=-20\) , and the cross terms give \(-15x+8x=-7x\) . Dividing by \(3x+4\) cancels that factor and leaves \(2x-5\) .

whyWrong.A: \(2x+5\) gives \((3x+4)(2x+5)=6x^{2}+23x+20\) , the wrong middle and constant terms.
whyWrong.C: \(3x-5\) pairs \(3x\) with \(3x\) , producing \(9x^{2}\) instead of \(6x^{2}\) .
whyWrong.D: \(2x-4\) gives a constant of 4(-4) = -16, not -20.

tips: Multiply the constants of your two factors first — they must give -20 here, which rules out two choices immediately.

whyCorrect: The model is a downward parabola, so the greatest yield is at its vertex, \(n=-\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{192}{2(-8)}=12\) . At n = 12 the yield is \(-8(144)+192(12)-300=852\) litres, more than any other value.

whyWrong.A: 6 gives J(6) = 564 litres, well below the peak.
whyWrong.B: 8 gives J(8) = 724 litres.
whyWrong.C: 10 gives J(10) = 820 litres — closer, but still short of 852.

tips: For \(ax^{2}+bx+c\) the vertex is always at \(-\frac{b}{2a}\) ; note the 2 in the denominator, not 4.

whyWrong.A: After 3 days the activity is 50 becquerels.
whyWrong.B: After 4 days the activity is 10 becquerels.
whyWrong.D: After 6 days the activity is 0.4 becquerels — one division too far.

tips: Recognise the powers of 5 (25, 125, 625, 3,125) and this becomes a counting exercise.

whyCorrect: Set the two expressions equal: \(x^{2}+4x-7=6x+8\) , which rearranges to \(x^{2}-2x-15=0\) . The sum of the roots is \(-\frac{b}{a}=2\) . (Factoring gives x = 5 and x = -3, which do sum to 2.)

whyWrong.A: -15 is the product of the two x-coordinates, the constant term of \(x^{2}-2x-15\) .
whyWrong.C: 5 is one of the two x-coordinates on its own; the other is -3.
whyWrong.D: 8 is the cable's y-intercept, not an x-coordinate of an intersection.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to move 6x to the left, which leaves \(x^{2}+4x-15\) and the wrong sum.

whyCorrect: Undo each operation in reverse. From \(F=\frac{5g-8}{3}\) , multiply by 3 to get 3F = 5g - 8, add 8 to get 3F + 8 = 5g, and divide by 5: \(g=\frac{3F+8}{5}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{3F-8}{5}\) subtracts the 8 again instead of adding it back.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{5F+8}{3}\) multiplies by 5 and divides by 3, reversing which number does which job.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{5F-8}{3}\) is the original formula with the letters swapped, not solved.

tips: Test with a number: g = 4 gives F = 4, and only choice D sends F = 4 back to g = 4.

whyCorrect: Complete the square: \(3x^{2}-12x+5=3(x^{2}-4x)+5=3(x-2)^{2}-12+5=3(x-2)^{2}-7\) . Since \(3(x-2)^{2}\) is never negative, the least value is -7, at x = 2.

whyWrong.B: -5 comes from subtracting 10 rather than the correct \(3(2)^{2}=12\) when completing the square.
whyWrong.C: 2 is the x-value at which the minimum occurs, not the minimum itself.
whyWrong.D: 5 is h(0), the value at x = 0; the curve dips below that before turning.

tips: You can also get the minimum by evaluating h at \(x=-\frac{b}{2a}=2\) : 12 - 24 + 5 = -7.

whyCorrect: Each year the balance is multiplied by 0.82, so after 3 years it is \(12{,}500(0.82)^{3}\) . Year by year that is $10,250, then $8,405, then $6,892 (since \(0.82^{3}=0.551368\) ).

whyWrong.B: $7,175 corresponds to carrying about 83.1% forward each year rather than 82%.
whyWrong.C: $8,610 is close to the two-year value, $8,405 — it stops a year early.
whyWrong.D: $9,225 is 10,250(0.9): the first year's 18% cut, then only a 10% cut afterwards.

commonMistakes: Taking 18% of the original $12,500 three times, which gives $5,750; each year's cut is 18% of the current balance.

whyCorrect: 21 metres of cord is 21/3 = 7 times the 3-metre batch, and each batch needs 8 hanks, so 7(8) = 56 hanks are required. At $6.50 a hank that costs 56(6.50) = $364.

whyWrong.A: $273 corresponds to 42 hanks, which is 2 hanks per metre rather than \(\frac{8}{3}\) .
whyWrong.B: $312 corresponds to 48 hanks, six batches instead of seven.
whyWrong.C: $338 corresponds to 52 hanks, which is not a whole number of 8-hank batches.

tips: Convert to whole batches first; the numbers stay integers and the arithmetic stays clean.

whyCorrect: Revenue is fare times journeys, so the two changes multiply: the fare becomes 0.85 of what it was and the journeys become 1.40 of what they were. That gives 0.85(1.40) = 1.19, so revenue is 119% of the original.

whyWrong.A: 102% treats the two changes as almost cancelling; a 15% cut and a 40% rise are taken on different quantities and do not offset.
whyWrong.C: 125% adds the percents, 100 - 15 + 40, instead of multiplying the factors.
whyWrong.D: 140% counts only the rise in journeys and ignores the fare cut entirely.

tips: Percent changes to two factors of a product always multiply; they never add.

whyCorrect: Multiply each kiln's count by its own percent and add: Aldon 0.08(250) = 20, Beck 0.05(180) = 9, Cray 0.10(320) = 32, Dell 0.04(150) = 6. The total is 20 + 9 + 32 + 6 = 67.

whyWrong.B: 71 comes from taking Cray's 10% of 360 rather than of 320, giving 36 instead of 32.
whyWrong.C: 76 applies Dell's row at 10% (15 pots) instead of its own 4% (6 pots).
whyWrong.D: 82 overstates more than one row; the four exact products are 20, 9, 32 and 6, and no correct combination of them exceeds 67.

commonMistakes: Averaging the four percents and applying one rate to all 900 pots, which ignores that the kilns fired different numbers.

whyCorrect: Convert both means into totals: the first 8 days brought 8(4.5) = 36 millimetres, and the first 12 days brought 12(5.25) = 63. Days 9 through 12 therefore account for 63 - 36 = 27 millimetres over 4 days, a mean of 27/4 = 6.75 millimetres.
commonMistakes: Subtracting the two means (5.25 - 4.5 = 0.75) — means over different numbers of days cannot be subtracted directly.
tips: Totals subtract; means do not.

whyCorrect: The three angles total 180° , so K + L = 180 - 40 = 140. With K = 3L, that gives 3L + L = 140, so L = 35 and K = 3(35) = 105.

whyWrong.A: 35 is angle L, the smaller of the two unknown angles.
whyWrong.B: 70 halves 140, which would be right only if K and L were equal.
whyWrong.D: 140 is the combined measure of K and L, before splitting it in the ratio 3 to 1.

tips: Subtract the known angle first, then split the remainder in the given ratio.

whyCorrect: The brace is the hypotenuse and the 12-metre wall height is the side opposite the 60° floor angle, so \(\sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{12}{L}\) . Then \(L=\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}/2}=\frac{24}{\sqrt{3}}=8\sqrt{3}\) metres, about 13.9.

whyWrong.A: \(4\sqrt{3}\) is \(\frac{12}{\tan 60^{\circ}}\) , the distance along the floor from the wall to the foot of the brace.
whyWrong.B: \(6\sqrt{3}\) multiplies 12 by \(\sin 60^{\circ}\) instead of dividing, which makes the hypotenuse shorter than a leg.
whyWrong.D: 24 uses \(\sin 30^{\circ}\) , the angle the brace makes with the wall rather than with the floor.

tips: The hypotenuse is the longest side, so any answer smaller than 12 here is wrong on sight.

whyCorrect: Every length is 3 times as large, so the volume scales by \(3^{3}=27\) . The statue therefore uses 27(350) = 9,450 cubic centimetres of bronze.
commonMistakes: Multiplying by 3 (1,050) or by 9 (3,150); volume scales by the cube of the length factor, not the factor or its square.

whyCorrect: Convert first: 27 litres is 27(1,000) = 27,000 cubic centimetres. For a cylinder the volume is the base area times the depth, so 1,800d = 27,000 and d = 15 centimetres.
commonMistakes: Trying to find the radius from the base area first — it is never needed, since the base area is already given.
tips: Volume divided by base area gives depth for any prism or cylinder.

whyCorrect: Set the expression equal to the fee: 5x - 13 = 42. Adding 13 gives 5x = 55, so x = 11 kilograms. Check: 5(11) - 13 = 55 - 13 = 42.

whyWrong.C: 10 gives 5(10) - 13 = $37, just short of $42.

commonMistakes: Subtracting the 13 instead of adding it, which gives (42 - 13)/5 = 5.8 and no listed answer.
tips: Undo the operations in reverse order: the -13 comes off last, so it is undone first.

whyCorrect: The mackerel cost 5(4) = $20, so the squid cost 65 - 20 = $45. At $9 a kilogram that is 45/9 = 5 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 4 kilograms of squid costs $36, for a total of $56.
whyWrong.C: 6 kilograms costs $54, for a total of $74.
whyWrong.D: 9 is the price per kilogram of squid, not the number of kilograms.

tips: Take off the part you can compute directly, then divide the remainder by the unit price.

whyCorrect: The book starts with 260 blank pages, and each day removes 3 of them, so after d days it has lost 3d pages. The number left is \(260-3d\) . Check with d = 10: 30 pages are filled, leaving 230, and 260 - 30 = 230.

whyWrong.B: \(260d-3\) attaches d to the starting total, so the book would gain pages as days pass.
whyWrong.C: \(3d-260\) reverses the subtraction and is negative for every small d.
whyWrong.D: \(263d\) adds 260 and 3 first, which multiplies the whole starting stock by the number of days.

tips: The quantity that repeats every day is the one multiplied by d.

whyCorrect: Set k = 0: a journey of no length still costs \(C(0)=1.80\) . That makes 1.80 the part of the fare charged regardless of distance, while 0.45 is the amount added per kilometre.

whyWrong.A: 1.80 is measured in dollars, not kilometres; the rule gives fares, not distances.
whyWrong.B: The charge per kilometre is 0.45, the number multiplied by k.
whyWrong.C: A 45-kilometre journey costs 1.80 + 0.45(45) = $22.05; the 45 in the choice comes from misreading 0.45.

tips: Substituting 0 for the variable isolates the constant term every time.

whyCorrect: "No more than 40" allows 40 and everything below it, and rules out only totals above 40. That is \(w\le 40\) .

whyWrong.A: \(w<40\) excludes exactly 40 submissions, which the gallery does allow.
whyWrong.C: \(w\ge 40\) allows 41 and above, the totals that stop the show going ahead.
whyWrong.D: \(w>40\) describes exactly when the show is not hung.

tips: Test the boundary value itself: 40 works are acceptable, so the boundary must be included.

whyCorrect: The 42 balcony seats are one third of the whole cinema, so the total is 3 times as large: 3(42) = 126 seats.

whyWrong.A: 14 divides 42 by 3, which finds a third of the balcony rather than the whole cinema.
whyWrong.B: 84 is the number of seats outside the balcony, the other two thirds.
whyWrong.D: 168 multiplies by 4 instead of 3.

commonMistakes: Dividing when the given amount is already the fraction — the part is smaller than the whole, so the whole comes from multiplying.

whyCorrect: In 6 hours the candle loses 6(2.5) = 15 centimetres. Starting from 30 centimetres, that leaves 30 - 15 = 15 centimetres.

whyWrong.A: 12 comes from burning 3 centimetres an hour: 30 - 18.
whyWrong.C: 18 comes from burning 2 centimetres an hour: 30 - 12.
whyWrong.D: 25 subtracts only 5 centimetres, the loss after 2 hours.

tips: Multiply rate by time first, then subtract once — not 2.5 taken off six separate times by hand.

whyCorrect: Add the two counts, matching like terms: \((5m+8)+(3m-2)\) gives 5m + 3m = 8m and 8 + (-2) = 6, so the total is \(8m+6\) .

whyWrong.B: \(8m+10\) adds 8 and 2 rather than combining +8 with -2.
whyWrong.C: \(2m+10\) subtracts the second expression instead of adding it.
whyWrong.D: \(15m-16\) multiplies the two expressions' parts instead of adding them.

tips: Watch the sign attached to each constant before combining them.

whyCorrect: The greatest common factor of \(6y^{2}\) and \(15y\) is 3y. Dividing gives \(6y^{2}\div 3y=2y\) and \(15y\div 3y=5\) , so the area factors as \(3y(2y-5)\) . Expanding it back returns \(6y^{2}-15y\) .

whyWrong.A: \(3y(2y+5)\) expands to \(6y^{2}+15y\) , with the wrong sign on the second term.
whyWrong.B: \(6y(y-15)\) expands to \(6y^{2}-90y\) — the 15 was not divided by the 6 taken out.
whyWrong.C: \(3y(2y-15)\) expands to \(6y^{2}-45y\) ; the 15 still needs dividing by the 3 that was factored out.

tips: Always expand your factored form back out; it catches an undivided term instantly.

whyWrong.A: 11 comes from 2(7) - 3, treating \(v^{2}\) as 2v.
whyWrong.B: 32 comes from mis-evaluating \(7^{2}\) as 35 (7 times 5) before subtracting 3.
whyWrong.D: 52 adds the 3 instead of subtracting it.

tips: Square first, then subtract — the exponent binds tighter than the subtraction.

whyCorrect: Solve \(2^{x}=64\) . Doubling from 1 gives 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 — that is six doublings, so x = 6.

whyWrong.A: 5 gives \(2^{5}=32\) times as large.
whyWrong.D: 32 halves 64, which is not what the exponent counts.

tips: Learn the powers of 2 up to 1,024; nearly every exponential SAT item uses one of them.

whyCorrect: Substitute d = 4 into \(L(d)=\frac{144}{d^{2}}\) . The denominator is \(4^{2}=16\) , so the illuminance is \(\frac{144}{16}=9\) lux.

whyWrong.B: 12 is \(\sqrt{144}\) , not the value of the model at d = 4.
whyWrong.C: 36 divides by 4 instead of by \(4^{2}\) , leaving the square undone.
whyWrong.D: 144 is the numerator, the value the model would give at d = 1.

commonMistakes: Squaring after dividing rather than before; only d is squared, not the whole fraction.

whyCorrect: Distribute the 4 across both terms: \(4(2p-3)=8p-12\) . Adding 5p gives 8p + 5p - 12 = \(13p-12\) .

whyWrong.B: \(13p-3\) multiplies 2p by 4 but leaves the -3 undistributed.
whyWrong.C: \(8p-12\) distributes correctly but drops the 5p entirely.
whyWrong.D: \(7p-12\) subtracts 5p instead of adding it.

tips: Distribute before combining, and check that every term inside the parentheses was multiplied.

whyCorrect: Substitute h = 3: \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}=\frac{1}{8}\) , so the amplitude is \(80\cdot\frac{1}{8}=10\) micrometres. Halving step by step gives the same thing: 80, 40, 20, 10.

whyWrong.B: 20 is the amplitude after 2 seconds — one halving short.
whyWrong.C: 40 is the amplitude after 1 second.
whyWrong.D: 77 subtracts 3 from 80 rather than halving three times.

tips: Exponential decay halves repeatedly; it never subtracts a fixed amount.

whyCorrect: Water is 5 parts and measures 45 litres, so one part is 45/5 = 9 litres. Woad is 3 parts, or 3(9) = 27 litres.

whyWrong.A: 15 divides 45 by 3, treating water as 3 parts rather than 5.
whyWrong.B: 21 would make one part 7 litres, but 45 litres over 5 parts makes a part 9 litres.
whyWrong.D: 75 flips the ratio, computing 45 times \(\frac{5}{3}\) — that would make woad the larger ingredient.

tips: The smaller number in the ratio must go with the smaller volume; 27 is less than 45, which is a quick sanity check.

whyCorrect: The stock fell by 250 - 210 = 40 helmets, and percent change is measured against the starting amount: 40/250 = 0.16, so the fall is 16 percent.

whyWrong.B: 20% divides the drop by 200 rather than by the starting stock of 250.
whyWrong.C: 25% divides the drop by 160.
whyWrong.D: 40% mistakes the drop of 40 helmets for a percentage.

commonMistakes: Dividing by the ending stock (40/210, about 19%) instead of the starting stock.

whyCorrect: Add the four values in the rainfall column: 62 + 48 = 110, then 110 + 35 = 145, then 145 + 41 = 186 millimetres.

whyWrong.A: 176 is 10 short, the result of a carrying slip in the first pair (62 + 48 = 110, not 100).
whyWrong.C: 196 is 10 too many, as if June had been read as 45 instead of 35.
whyWrong.D: 206 is 20 too many, as if two of the values had been rounded up to the next ten.

tips: Add in pairs and re-add in the opposite order; the two totals must agree.

whyCorrect: Put the lengths in order first: 38, 42, 50, 55, 61, 66, 74. With seven values the median is the 4th, which has three lengths below and three above. That is 55 centimetres.
commonMistakes: Taking the middle of the list as written (61) without sorting, or computing the mean (about 55.1) instead.

whyCorrect: The wall is a straight line, so the two angles the path makes with it on either side lie on that line and add to 180° . The other angle is 180 - 63 = 117 degrees.

whyWrong.A: 27 subtracts from 90° , which applies to complementary angles, not angles on a straight line.
whyWrong.B: 63 would mean both angles are equal, which happens only when the path meets the wall at a right angle.
whyWrong.D: 243 subtracts from 306° ; the two angles on one side of a straight line total 180° .

tips: Angles on a straight line sum to 180° ; angles all the way round a point sum to 360° .

whyCorrect: The area of a circle is \(\pi r^{2}\) , so with r = 9 the area is \(\pi(9)^{2}=81\pi\) square metres.

whyWrong.A: \(9\pi\) uses r instead of \(r^{2}\) .
whyWrong.B: \(18\pi\) is \(2\pi r\) , the circumference, which is a length rather than an area.
whyWrong.D: \(162\pi\) doubles the correct area, combining the circumference formula's 2 with the squared radius.

tips: Areas carry squared units, so the radius must appear squared.

whyCorrect: The volume of a rectangular prism is length times width times height: 4(3)(5) = 60 cubic feet.
commonMistakes: Computing surface area instead, 2(12) + 2(20) + 2(15) = 94 square feet.

whyCorrect: The two arms meet at a right angle, so they are the legs of a right triangle and the batten is the hypotenuse. Then \(9^{2}+12^{2}=81+144=225\) , and the batten is \(\sqrt{225}=15\) centimetres.
commonMistakes: Adding the arms to get 21; the hypotenuse is always shorter than the sum of the legs.
tips: 9, 12, 15 is the 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 3 — worth recognising on sight.

whyCorrect: If every solution of the first equation also solves the second, the two equations describe the same line, so one is a multiple of the other. The x-terms give the factor: 9 is \(\frac{3}{2}\) of 6, and the constants agree, since 21 is \(\frac{3}{2}\) of 14. So \(k=\frac{3}{2}(-4)=-6\) .

whyWrong.B: -4 copies the first equation's y-coefficient without scaling it by \(\frac{3}{2}\) .
whyWrong.C: 4 scales the size correctly but loses the negative sign.
whyWrong.D: 6 has the right size and the wrong sign; multiplying -4 by a positive factor stays negative.

tips: Check all three coefficients against the same factor — x, y and the constant must all scale alike.

whyCorrect: The slope is \(\frac{-7-11}{5-(-1)}=\frac{-18}{6}=-3\) . From x = 5 to x = 9 is a run of 4, so the output falls by 3(4) = 12: \(f(9)=-7-12=-19\) .

whyWrong.B: -13 uses a run of 2 instead of the 4 units from 5 to 9.
whyWrong.C: -7 is \(f(5)\) , left unchanged.
whyWrong.D: 5 adds 12 rather than subtracting it, treating the slope as +3.

tips: Watch the sign of the slope through both the subtraction and the final step; two sign slips here cancel into a plausible-looking answer.

whyCorrect: Each bench forces at least 3 stools, so a bench really costs 8 + 3(3) = 17 board-feet of the stock. With at most 240 board-feet, \(17b\le 240\) gives b at most 14.1, so 14 benches: 14 benches and 42 stools use 112 + 126 = 238 board-feet.

whyWrong.A: 10 benches with 30 stools use only 170 board-feet, leaving 70 — enough for four more benches and their stools.
whyWrong.B: 12 benches with 36 stools use 204 board-feet, leaving 36, enough for two more bench-and-stools groups.
whyWrong.C: 13 benches with 39 stools use 221 board-feet, leaving 19, still enough for one more group of 17.

tips: Bundle the forced items with the item you are maximising, then divide once.

whyCorrect: In its 2-hour head start the tug covers 2(14) = 28 kilometres. The launch closes that gap at 21 - 14 = 7 kilometres per hour, so it takes 28/7 = 4 hours to draw level. In those 4 hours the launch travels 4(21) = 84 kilometres from the jetty.

whyWrong.A: 56 is how far the tug travels during the 4-hour chase; add its 28-kilometre head start to get 84.
whyWrong.C: 98 multiplies the tug's 14 km/h by the 7 km/h speed difference, which mixes two different quantities.
whyWrong.D: 126 is 21 times 6, using the tug's total 6 hours of travel with the launch's speed.

commonMistakes: Setting 14t = 21t, which has no useful solution; the two boats travel for different lengths of time, so one time must be t and the other t - 2.
tips: Either equate distances with offset times, or use the closing-speed shortcut — both give 84.

whyCorrect: A 130-kilometre delivery has 90 kilometres beyond the first 40, and those cost 455 - 95 = $360, so the rate is 360/90 = $4 per kilometre. A 200-kilometre delivery has 160 kilometres beyond the first 40, costing 95 + 4(160) = 95 + 640 = $735.
commonMistakes: Charging $4 for all 200 kilometres ($800) or scaling $455 by \(\frac{200}{130}\) — the first 40 kilometres are priced separately and only once.
tips: Subtract the flat portion from both the distance and the cost before finding the rate.

whyCorrect: Adding the two equations gives 8a + 8c = 88, so a + c = 11 directly — you never need the individual prices. (For a check: subtracting gives a - c = 3, so a = 7 and c = 4, and 3(7) + 5(4) = 41.)

whyWrong.A: 8 comes from dividing 88 by 11 instead of by the 8 that multiplies both variables.
whyWrong.C: 16 would need a pair such as a = 7 and c = 9, which fails the first equation (21 + 45 = 66, not 41).
whyWrong.D: 22 divides 88 by 4 rather than by 8.

tips: When a system is symmetric like this, adding the equations gives a + c and subtracting gives a - c in one step each.

whyCorrect: Substitute the temperature range into \(T=25r+540\) : \(940\le 25r+540\le 1{,}060\) . Subtracting 540 throughout gives \(400\le 25r\le 520\) , and dividing by 25 gives \(16\le r\le 20.8\) .

whyWrong.A: \(15.2\le r\le 19.2\) corresponds to temperatures of 920 and 1,020 degrees, not 940 and 1,060.
whyWrong.B: The lower bound is right, but r = 21.2 gives T = 1,070 degrees, above the allowed maximum.
whyWrong.C: \(37.6\) and \(42.4\) divide the temperatures by 25 without first subtracting the 540.

tips: Undo the +540 before the times-25, and apply each step to all three parts of the inequality.

whyCorrect: First \(q(3)=3^{2}-2=7\) . Feeding 7 into p gives \(p(7)=7a+7\) , and this equals 35, so 7a = 28 and a = 4.

whyWrong.C: 7 is the output of q, the number fed into p, not the constant a.
whyWrong.D: 28 is the value of 7a, one division short of a.

commonMistakes: Feeding 3 into p instead of into q; the order stated is q first, then p.

whyCorrect: Factor both parts: \(2x^{2}-18=2(x^{2}-9)=2(x-3)(x+3)\) and \(x^{2}+6x+9=(x+3)^{2}\) . One factor of \(x+3\) cancels, leaving \(\frac{2(x-3)}{x+3}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{2(x+3)}{x-3}\) cancels the wrong factor, inverting which binomial survives.
whyWrong.B: \(2x-6\) cancels \(x+3\) twice, as though the denominator were \(x+3\) rather than \((x+3)^{2}\) .
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{2x-18}{x+3}\) factors the 2 out of only the first term of the numerator.

tips: Factor numerator and denominator completely before cancelling anything — cancelling term by term is what produces these wrong forms.

whyCorrect: Write the profile in vertex form: \(x^{2}-6x+13=(x-3)^{2}+4\) . A horizontal line meets this upward parabola exactly once only at its lowest point, so k = 4. (Equivalently, \(x^{2}-6x+13-k=0\) has one root when its discriminant \(36-4(13-k)\) is 0.)

whyWrong.A: 3 is the x-coordinate of the vertex, not its height.
whyWrong.C: 9 is the number subtracted while completing the square, not the minimum value.
whyWrong.D: 13 is the value at x = 0; the line y = 13 crosses the profile at two points.

tips: One intersection with a horizontal line always means the vertex — no discriminant work needed once you have vertex form.

whyCorrect: Let w be the width; the length is w + 7, so \(w(w+7)=330\) , giving \(w^{2}+7w-330=0\) and \((w-15)(w+22)=0\) . The width is 15 and the length 22, so the perimeter is 2(15 + 22) = 74 metres.

whyWrong.A: 44 is 2(22), counting only the pair of longer sides.
whyWrong.B: 64 needs the two dimensions to total 32, which with a difference of 7 gives an area of about 244, not 330.
whyWrong.D: 82 needs the dimensions to total 41, giving 17 by 24 and an area of 408.

commonMistakes: Stopping at the width, 15, or at the length, 22 — the question asks for the perimeter.

whyWrong.A: \(3b^{2}\) makes both errors: leaving 27 unraised and subtracting the exponents wrongly.
whyWrong.B: \(3b^{3}\) treats \(27^{\frac{4}{3}}\) as 27, giving 27/9 = 3 instead of 81/9 = 9.
whyWrong.C: \(9b^{2}\) has the coefficient right but takes 8 - 5 as 2 rather than 3.

tips: A fractional exponent means root then power: the cube root of 27 is 3, and \(3^{4}=81\) .

whyCorrect: Use the given point to find c: at x = 0, \(s(0)=\frac{1}{50}(0-30)^{2}+c=\frac{900}{50}+c=18+c\) , and that equals 20, so c = 2. Then \(s(50)=\frac{1}{50}(50-30)^{2}+2=\frac{400}{50}+2=8+2=10\) metres.

whyWrong.A: 8 is the \(\frac{1}{50}(20)^{2}\) term with the constant c never added.
whyWrong.C: 12 corresponds to c = 4, which would put the cable 22 metres above the deck at x = 0.
whyWrong.D: 18 is \(\frac{1}{50}(30)^{2}\) , the value at x = 0 without c, so it answers for the wrong position.

tips: Solve for the unknown constant first; everything after that is a single substitution.

whyCorrect: The starting mass 12 multiplies the growth factor, and the factor is 3 per 5-hour period, so the exponent must count periods: t hours is \(\frac{t}{5}\) periods. That gives \(12\cdot 3^{\frac{t}{5}}\) , which returns 12 at t = 0 and 36 at t = 5.

whyWrong.B: \(12\cdot 5^{\frac{t}{3}}\) swaps the growth factor with the length of the period, tripling the exponent's meaning.
whyWrong.C: \(12\cdot 3^{5t}\) triples five times every hour instead of once every five hours.
whyWrong.D: \(3\cdot 12^{\frac{t}{5}}\) swaps the starting mass with the growth factor, giving a mass of 3 grams at t = 0.

tips: Test t = 0 and t = 5 on any exponential model choice; that alone eliminates three options here.

whyCorrect: Convert each mean to a total: 14(4.2) = 58.8 kilograms and 6(5.7) = 34.2 kilograms. All 20 salmon weigh 93 kilograms, so the overall mean is 93/20 = 4.65 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 4.35 corresponds to a combined mass of 87 kilograms, less than the tanks actually hold.
whyWrong.B: 4.5 corresponds to a combined mass of 90 kilograms.
whyWrong.D: 4.95 is the plain average of 4.2 and 5.7, which ignores that the first tank holds more than twice as many salmon.

commonMistakes: Averaging two means directly; that is only valid when the groups are the same size.
tips: The combined mean must lie closer to the mean of the larger group — 4.65 is nearer 4.2, as it should be.

whyCorrect: "Of the holders who grow soft fruit" restricts you to that column: 54 + 96 = 150 people. Of those, 54 keep bees, so the fraction is \(\frac{54}{150}=\frac{9}{25}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{9}{40}\) is \(\frac{54}{240}\) , using all 240 surveyed holders as the denominator.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{27}{40}\) is \(\frac{54}{80}\) , the fraction of bee-keepers who grow soft fruit — the reverse of what is asked.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{5}{8}\) is \(\frac{150}{240}\) , the share of all holders who grow soft fruit.

tips: The phrase after "of the" names the denominator; find that group's total before anything else.

whyCorrect: The wagon holds 13.5(1,000) = 13,500 kilograms. At 45 kilograms a minute that takes 13,500/45 = 300 minutes, and 300 minutes is 300/60 = 5 hours.

whyWrong.A: 3 hours is 180 minutes and delivers only 8,100 kilograms.
whyWrong.B: 4 hours is 240 minutes and delivers 10,800 kilograms.
whyWrong.D: 6 hours is 360 minutes and would deliver 16,200 kilograms, more than the wagon holds.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the final minutes-to-hours conversion and answering 300.
tips: Convert tonnes to kilograms first so the rate's units match the amount's.

whyCorrect: In the sample, 21 of 60 gulls exceeded 140 centimetres, a proportion of 21/60 = 0.35. Applying that proportion to the whole colony gives 0.35(900) = 315 gulls.
commonMistakes: Multiplying 21 by 900/60 = 15 is the same calculation and also gives 315; multiplying 21 by 900 or dividing 900 by 21 does not.
tips: Set up the proportion 21/60 = x/900 and cross-multiply if the shortcut feels risky.

whyCorrect: Since \(DE\) is parallel to \(BC\) , triangles \(ADE\) and \(ABC\) are similar. The scale factor is \(\frac{AD}{AB}=\frac{6}{6+9}=\frac{6}{15}=\frac{2}{5}\) , so \(DE=\frac{2}{5}BC\) . Then \(BC=8\cdot\frac{5}{2}=20\) feet.

whyWrong.A: 12 uses the ratio \(\frac{DB}{AD}=\frac{9}{6}\) , but the similar triangles compare AD with the whole side AB, not with DB.
whyWrong.B: 14 adds 6 to 8, treating the segments as lengths to be summed rather than scaled.
whyWrong.D: 24 uses a scale factor of 3; the correct factor is \(\frac{15}{6}=2.5\) .

commonMistakes: Using AD to DB (6 to 9) instead of AD to AB (6 to 15) as the ratio.

whyCorrect: The cylinder holds \(\pi r^{2}h=\pi(9)(5)=45\pi\) cubic metres. The cone holds \(\frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h=\frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(4)=12\pi\) . The total is \(45\pi+12\pi=57\pi\) .

whyWrong.A: \(45\pi\) is the cylinder alone, with the cone left off.
whyWrong.C: \(69\pi\) uses \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the cone's enclosing cylinder (24\(\pi\) ) instead of \(\frac{1}{3}\) .
whyWrong.D: \(81\pi\) treats the cone as a full cylinder, \(36\pi\) , forgetting the factor \(\frac{1}{3}\) .

tips: A cone is exactly one third of the cylinder with the same base and height.

whyCorrect: The right angle is at N, so the hypotenuse is \(LM=\sqrt{24^{2}+7^{2}}=\sqrt{576+49}=\sqrt{625}=25\) . For angle L, the adjacent leg is \(LN=24\) , so \(\cos L=\frac{24}{25}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{7}{24}\) is \(\tan L\) , opposite over adjacent.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{7}{25}\) is \(\sin L\) , the opposite leg over the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{24}{7}\) inverts the tangent; a cosine can never exceed 1.

tips: Any sine or cosine bigger than 1 is wrong on sight — that alone rules out one choice here.

whyCorrect: No metal is lost, so the two solids have equal volume. The cube holds \(10^{3}=1{,}000\) cubic centimetres, and the block holds 25(8)h = 200h. Setting 200h = 1,000 gives h = 5.
commonMistakes: Matching surface areas instead of volumes; recasting preserves volume, not surface area.
